“Kiss me, Kristin, my betrothed!” Then she would think he was speaking in delirium. No, Kristin. She would be surprised.

Erlend had understood it. Ramborg had understood it. But Kristin—she sat there with her sorrow and anger—as angry and bitter as she was now with that man Erlend, she still had no thought for anyone but him. You have never cared enough about me, Kristin, my beloved, to wonder whether it was hard for me when I had to be a brother to the woman who had once been promised to me as my wife—.

He himself had not known it then, when he parted from her outside the convent gate in Oslo—that he would go on thinking of her in this way. That in the end he would feel that nothing he had received in life afterward was full compensation for what he had lost then. For the maiden who had been pledged to me in my youth.

She should hear it before he died. She should give him one kiss—.

—I am the one who loved you and who still loves you—.

He had heard those words once, and he had never been able to forget them. They were from the book of the Virgin Mary’s miracles; it was a tale of a nun who fled her convent with a knight. The maiden Mary—she saved those two in the end and forgave them despite their sin. If it was a sin for him to say this to his wife’s sister before he died, then the Mother of God must obtain forgiveness for him for this as well. It was not often that he had troubled her by asking her for anything—.

—I did not believe it myself then, that I would never again be truly glad or merry—.

“No, Simon, it is too much for Sokka if she must carry both of us—as far as she has had to run tonight,” he said to the man who had mounted behind him and was supporting him. “I can see that it is you, Sigurd, but I thought you were someone else—”

They reached the pilgrims’ hospice toward morning, and the two monks who managed the place took charge of the sick man. But when he had revived somewhat under their care and the feverish delirium had abated, Simon Andressøn stubbornly insisted on borrowing a sleigh and traveling farther north.

The going was good, and they changed horses on the way; they traveled through the whole night and reached Formo at daybreak the next morning. Simon had lain dozing beneath everything they had spread over him. It pressed upon him so heavily—at times he felt as if he were being crushed beneath massive slabs of rock—and his head hurt so badly. Now and then he seemed to lose consciousness. Then the pains began raging through him again—it was as if his body swelled and swelled, became inconceivably large, and was about to burst into pieces. His arm throbbed and throbbed—.

He tried to walk from the sleigh into the house—with his sound arm across Jon’s shoulder, while Sigurd walked behind to support him. Simon noticed that the men’s faces were gray and grimy with exhaustion—they had sat in the saddle for two nights running. He wanted to say something to them about it, but his tongue would not obey him. At the threshold he stumbled and fell headlong into the room—with a roar of pain when his monstrously swollen arm struck against something. Sweat streamed from him as he swallowed the groans that tried to escape while he was undressed and helped into bed.

Not long afterward he saw Kristin Lavransdatter standing by the stove, pounding something with a club in a wooden bowl. The sound went straight through his head. She poured from a small pot into a cup and dripped drops into it from a glass bottle that she took from her chest—emptied what she had crushed in the bowl into the pot and set it by the fire. So quiet and deft were her ways—.

Now she came to the bed with the cup in her hand. She walked so lightly. She was as erect and beautiful as the maiden had been, the slender mistress of the house with the lean, grave face beneath her linen headdress. He was swollen at the back of his neck too; it hurt when she slipped one arm beneath him and raised him a little. She supported his head against her breast while holding the cup to his mouth with her left hand.

Simon smiled a little, and when she carefully let his head sink back onto the pillows, he grasped one of her hands with his sound hand. It was no longer soft or white, that fine, long, narrow woman’s hand.

“You can scarcely sew silk with these fingers of yours now,” said Simon. “But they are good and gentle—and delightfully cool is your hand, Kristin!” He laid it on his forehead. Kristin remained standing so until she felt her palm grow warm; then she changed hands and gently pressed the other against his burning forehead, all the way up beneath the roots of his hair.

“Your arm is in a bad state, Simon,” she said. “But with God’s help it may go well.”

“I fear, Kristin, that you cannot heal me, however skillful a healer you are,” said Simon. But his expression was almost cheerful. The drink was beginning to take effect; he felt the pains much less. But his eyes felt so strange—as though he could not control them—he thought he must surely be lying there squinting, one eye in each direction—.

“It will go with me as it is ordained,” he said as before.

Kristin returned to her pots—spread a paste on linen cloths, came back, and wrapped the hot bandages around his arm from the fingertips, all around behind his back and forward across his chest, where the swelling ran in red streaks from the armpit. It hurt at first, but soon brought relief. She wrapped woolen cloths over them and placed soft down pillows beneath the arm. Simon asked what she had put on the bandages.

“Oh, various things—comfrey root and celandine,” said Kristin. “If only it had been summer, so I could have taken them fresh from my herb garden. But I had plenty—thanks be to God—I have not needed any before this winter.”

“What was it you once told me about celandine—you had heard it from the abbess when you were in the convent—about the name—”

“Do you mean that in every tongue it has a name signifying swallow-flower—from the Greek Sea all the way here to the Northern Lands?”

“Yes—because it bursts into bloom in every country when the swallows awaken from their winter sleep?” Simon pressed his lips a little more firmly together. By then he would already have lain long in the earth—.

“I want my resting place by the church here,” he said, “if it should happen that I die now, Kristin. I am now so rich a man that Andres will likely one day sit with some authority here at Formo. I wonder whether it will be a son that Ramborg bears me this spring—I should gladly have lived long enough to see two sons in my house—”

Kristin said that she had sent word south to Dyfrin that he had fallen so ill. Gaute—he had already ridden off that morning.

“You did not send the child away alone?” Simon asked in alarm.

She had had no one at hand whom she thought capable of keeping pace with Gaute on Rauden, she answered. Simon said it would be a hard journey for Ramborg—if only she did not hurry more than she could bear. “But I should dearly like to see my children—”

A little later he began speaking of his children again. He mentioned Arngjerd—whether he had done wrong when he refused that offer from the people of Eiken. But the man had seemed too old to him—and he had feared that Grunde was said to be somewhat violent when drunk. Arngjerd was the one he had wanted to place in the safest circumstances. Now Gyrd and Gudmund would have charge of her marriage. “Tell my brothers, Kristin—I sent them greeting; they must take great care in this matter. If you would take her over to Jørundgaard for a while, I shall thank you where I lie. And if Ramborg marries again before Arngjerd is provided for, then you must take her to you, Kristin. You must not think that Ramborg has ever been anything but kind to her—but if she is to have both a stepmother and a stepfather, I fear she may be regarded more as a serving-woman than as—you remember, I was married to Halfrid when I became her father—”

Kristin gently laid her hand upon Simon’s and promised that she would do everything in her power for the maiden. She remembered all she had seen—how difficult their position was, those children who had a great lord for their father and had been begotten in adultery. Orm and Margret, Ulf Haldorssøn—. She kept stroking Simon’s hand.

“It is not yet certain that you will die this time, brother-in-law,” she said, smiling a little. Even now a reflection of the maiden’s sweet, gentle smile could pass over the lean, stern face of the matron. You sweet young Kristin—.

Simon did not develop such a high fever that evening, and he said he felt less pain. When Kristin changed the bandage on his arm, it was not so swollen; the flesh was softer, and the marks of her fingers remained for a while when she carefully pressed it.

Kristin sent the servants to bed. Jon Daalk, who insisted on keeping watch over his master, she allowed to lie down on the bench. She had the chest-bench with the carved back moved forward before the bed and placed there, leaning into the corner. Simon dozed and slept—once, when he awakened, he saw that she had found herself a distaff. She sat very erect, with the staff and its head of wool tucked beneath her left arm; her fingers twisted the thread, the spindle sank and sank beside her long, slender lap—then she wound up the thread, twisted again, and the spindle sank—he fell asleep watching it—.

When he awakened again toward morning, she was still sitting there spinning. The light from the candle, which she had placed so that the bed-curtain shaded him, fell directly on her face. It was so pale and still; the full, soft mouth had become narrow and firmly closed, and she sat with lowered eyes, spinning. She could not see that he lay awake, staring at her from the shadow of the bed-hangings. She looked so utterly sorrowful that Simon felt as though his heart were bleeding as he lay watching her.

She rose and went to tend the fire. So silently. When she returned, she peered behind the bed-curtain—and met his open eyes in the darkness.

“How is it with you now, Simon?” she asked softly.

“Well—it is well with me now.”

But he thought he could feel tenderness beneath his left arm now as well—and beneath his chin when he moved his head. No, surely it was only something he imagined—.

Oh, she would surely never feel that she had lost anything when she rejected his love—for that reason he might safely tell her of it. It could not possibly make her more melancholy. He would tell her before he died—just once: I have loved you through all these years—.

The fever rose again. And his left arm hurt—.

“You must try to sleep again, Simon. Perhaps you will soon improve,” she said quietly.

“I have slept a great deal tonight—” He began speaking of his children again—the three he had and loved so dearly—and the unborn one. Then he fell silent—the pains returned so fiercely. “Lie down for a while now, Kristin. Jon can surely sit up for a time, if you think someone must keep watch.”

In the morning, when she unwrapped the bandage, Simon looked calmly up into her despairing face. “No, Kristin, there was already too much corruption and uncleanness in the arm—and I had been chilled through before I came into your hands. I told you that you cannot heal me. Do not grieve so over this, Kristin!”

“You should not have traveled the whole long road,” she said faintly.

“No man lives longer than he is ordained to,” Simon answered as before. “I wanted to come home—. There are one or two things to speak of—how matters are to be arranged after me.”

He laughed a little.

“All fires burn out at last.”

Kristin looked at him with tear-bright eyes. He had always had so many proverbs on his lips. She looked down into his red-blotched face. The heavy cheeks and the folds beneath his chin seemed to have collapsed and lay in deep creases. His eyes seemed both dull and shining—then clarity and thought appeared in them again: he looked up at her with the firm, searching gaze that had most often been in those small, sharp, steel-gray eyes.

When full daylight filled the room, Kristin saw that Simon had grown thin around the nose—a strip of white ran down toward each corner of his mouth.

She went to the little glass pane and stood there swallowing her tears. The thick frost on the window glittered and shone golden-green. Outside it was surely as beautiful a winter day as it had been all week—.

It was the sign of death, she knew—.

She came back and slipped her hand beneath the coverlet—he was swollen about the ankles and upward along the calves.

“Will you—will you have us send for Sira Eirik now?” she asked softly.

“Yes, this evening,” answered Simon.

He had to speak of it before he confessed and received the sacrament. Afterward he must try to turn his thoughts elsewhere.

“It is strange that it will surely be you who must tend my corpse,” said Simon. “And I fear I shall not make a very handsome corpse.”

Kristin choked back a sob. She went to prepare another cooling drink. But Simon said:

“I do not like these drinks of yours, Kristin—my thoughts grow so clouded afterward.”

A little later he asked her to give him some after all.

“But do not put too much of the stupefying thing in it. I must speak with you about a matter.”

He drank and lay waiting for the pains to ease enough that he could speak clearly and calmly with her.

“Would you not have us fetch Sira Eirik to you—so that he may speak to you such words as might now give you consolation?”

“Yes, soon. But there is something I should have told you first.”

He lay still for a little. Then he said:

“Tell Erlend Nikulaussøn that I have regretted every day since the last words I spoke to him when we parted. Unmanly and small-minded was my conduct toward my brother-in-law that night. Give him my greeting and say—ask him to forgive me for it.”

Kristin sat with bowed head—Simon saw her turn blood-red beneath her linen headdress.

“You will carry this message to your husband?” he asked.

She nodded slightly. Then Simon said again:

“If Erlend does not come to my funeral feast, you must seek him out, Kristin, and tell him this.”

Kristin sat silent, her face dark red.

“You will not refuse to do what I ask of you, now that I am to die?” asked Simon Andressøn.

“No,” whispered the woman. “I shall—do it—”

“It is bad for your sons, Kristin, that there is enmity between their father and mother,” Simon resumed. “I wonder whether you have seen how greatly this torments them. It is hard for those fine lads to know that their parents are on everyone’s tongue throughout the district.”

Kristin answered harshly and in a low voice:

“Erlend left our sons—not I. First my sons lost their foothold in the districts where birth and ancestral property entitled them to stand. If they must now endure village gossip about their home here in the valley from which I come—I did not cause it.”

Simon lay silent for a while. Then he said:

“I do not forget that, Kristin—you have a right to complain of many things—Erlend has provided badly for his own. But you must remember—had his undertaking succeeded, his sons would now have been well secured, and he himself would have stood among the mightiest knights in this realm. A man is called a traitor to his sovereign when he fails in such a matter—but when he succeeds, people speak very differently. Half of Norway thought as Erlend did then—that we were ill served by sharing a king with the Swedes, and that there was likely different mettle in Knut Porse’s son than in this pampered boy, if we could have brought young lord Haakon to us in his infancy. Many stood behind Erlend then and pulled the rope with him—they slipped away and hid when the matter came to light—my own brothers did so, and many others who are now called good knights and men-at-arms. Erlend alone had to fall. And then, Kristin, your husband showed that he was a noble and courageous man—whatever his conduct may have been before and since—”

Kristin sat still, trembling.

“I think, Kristin, if it was on account of this matter that you spoke bitter words to your husband, you must swallow them again. You of all women should be able to do so, Kristin—once you held fast enough to Erlend—you could not bear to hear one true word about his conduct toward you, when he acted in such a way that I could never have believed an honorable man capable of it, still less a highborn lord and courteous retainer—do you remember when I came upon you in Oslo? You could forgive Erlend for that, both then and afterward—”

Kristin answered quietly:

“I had cast my lot in with his then—what would have become of me afterward if I had separated my cause from Erlend’s?”

“Look at me, Kristin,” said Simon Darre, “and answer me truthfully. If I had held your father to the word he had given—chosen to take you as you were—if I had told you that I would never remind you of your shame, but that I would not release you—what would you have done then?”

“I do not know.”

Simon laughed harshly:

“If I had forced my way to drinking my wedding feast with you—you would scarcely have taken me willingly into your arms, Kristin, my fair one—”

Now her face had turned white. She sat looking down and did not answer. He laughed as before:

“I do not think you would have welcomed me gently when I entered the bridal bed with you—”

“I think I would have taken a knife to bed with me,” she whispered, half choked.

“I hear that you know the ballad of Knut of Borg,” Simon said with a grim smile. “I have never heard of such a thing actually happening among people. But God knows whether you might not have done it!”

A little later he spoke again:

“It is also unheard of among Christian people for lawfully wedded folk to separate by their own will, as you two have done—without lawful cause or the bishop’s consent. Are you not ashamed? You trampled everything down and defied everything in order to come together; when Erlend was in mortal danger, you thought of nothing but saving him, and he thought far more of you than of his seven sons, his name, and his property. But as soon as you can possess one another in secure peace, you cannot preserve decency and concord—discord and discontent ruled between you at Husaby too; I saw it myself, Kristin—

“I tell you, for your sons’ sake you must seek reconciliation with your husband. If the lesser fault is yours, then it should also be easier for you to offer Erlend your hand,” he said more gently.

“It is easier for you than for Erlend Nikulaussøn, sitting up at Haugen in poverty,” Simon said again.

“It is not easy for me,” she whispered. “I think that I have at least shown I can do something for my children. I have struggled and struggled for them—”

“That is true,” said Simon. Then he asked, “Do you remember the day we met on the road near Nidaros? You sat in the grass nursing Naakkve—”

Kristin nodded.

“Could you have done for the child at your breast what my sister did for her son—handed him away to those better able to protect him?”

Kristin shook her head.

“But ask his father to forget what you may have said to him in anger—do you think you can do that for him and for six other fine sons—tell your husband that the young men need him to return home to them and to his estate?”

“I shall do as you wish, Simon,” said Kristin quietly.

“You have spoken to me about this in harsh terms,” she said a little later. “Before now, too, you have rebuked me more severely than any other layman—”

“But now I can promise you that this will be the last time,” his voice took on the teasing, cheerful ring it had had in earlier days. “No, do not weep so, Kristin—but remember, my sister, you have promised this to a dying man.”

Once more the old mischievous gleam came into his eyes.

“You know, Kristin—it has happened before that I learned you were not to be relied upon!”

“Be still now, dear one,” he begged a little later; he had lain listening to her broken, bitter weeping. “I remember that you were a good and faithful sister to us, you may be sure. Friends we became in the end, Kristin mine—”

Toward evening he asked them to fetch a priest. Sira Eirik came, heard his confession, gave him extreme unction and the viaticum. He took leave of his servants and of Erlend’s sons, the five who were at home—Kristin had sent Naakkve to Kruke—Simon had asked to see Kristin’s children and bid them farewell.

Kristin also kept watch over the dying man that night. Toward morning she fell asleep for a moment. She awoke at a strange sound—Simon lay softly moaning and lamenting. It seized her violently when she heard it—that he complained quietly and bitterly like a wretched, forsaken child, now that he thought no one could hear him. She bent down and kissed him many times upon the face. She could already smell the sickly, dead odor of his breath and his body. But when daylight came, she saw that his eyes were still alive and clear and steadfast.

He was suffering terrible pains, she understood, when Jon and Sigurd lifted him in a sheet while she tended his bed and made it as soft and comfortable as she could. He had wanted no food for a full day now, but he was very thirsty.

When she had settled him, he asked her to make the sign of the cross over him: “Now I cannot move my left arm either.”

—But when we sign ourselves with the cross, or anything that we wish to shelter beneath the cross, then we must remember why the cross was hallowed and what it signifies, and remember that through the Lord’s sufferings and death this sign received honor and power—

Simon remembered that he had once heard someone read this aloud. He had probably not been accustomed to thinking much when he crossed his breast or marked the cross upon his houses and property. He felt unprepared and ill equipped to depart from this world—he must comfort himself that he had made ready as well as time allowed, by confession, and that he had received the last sacrament. Ramborg—but she was so young; perhaps she would be far happier with another man. His children—God must take them into His keeping—and Gyrd would manage their welfare faithfully and wisely.

And then he must entrust himself to God, who judges a man not according to his worth but by His grace—.

Later that day Sigrid Andresdatter and Geirmund of Kruke arrived. Simon then wished Kristin to go out and rest, for she had watched over and tended him so long.

“And soon I shall be unpleasant to be near,” he said, smiling a little. Then she gave a piercing sob for a moment—and bent down to kiss once more the wretched body that had already begun to decay.

Simon lay quietly. The fever and the pains were now much less severe. He lay thinking that it could not be very long now before he was released.

He himself wondered that he had spoken to Kristin as he had. It was not what he had meant to tell her. But he had been unable to speak otherwise. At times he was almost vexed by it.

But now the gangrene must soon reach his heart. A man’s heart is the first thing to quicken in the mother’s womb and the last thing in him to grow still. But now it must soon be still within him—.

In the evening he lay delirious. A couple of times he cried aloud in torment, so that it was dreadful to hear. But at other times he lay laughing softly and mentioned his own name, Kristin thought—but Sigrid, who sat bent over him, whispered to her that he was probably speaking of a boy, their cousin, who had been such a good friend of his in childhood. Around midnight he grew calm and seemed to sleep. Then Sigrid persuaded Kristin to lie down for a while on the other bed in the room.

She awoke to movement in the room—it was shortly before dawn—and then she heard that the death struggle had begun. Simon had lost the power of speech, but he still knew her; she could see it in his eyes. Then it was as though steel broke within them—they rolled upward beneath the lids. Yet he lay for a while longer, rattling in his throat and still alive. The priest had come and was reading the prayers for the dying; the two women sat by the bed, and the whole household was in the room. A little before noon he finally breathed his last.
